# Results summary (generated by analysis/plots.py)

**fig1_before_after.** Before and after, in the live network (12 h, 10 test topologies, every setting pooled: 1 grayhole at two loads, 2 and 3 grayholes; 95% t-intervals over topologies). Each method runs with its own rule and the same response (delivery and throughput error bars: 95% t-interval of the difference from no defence on the same topology): a node flagged in two consecutive 30-min rounds stops being used as a relay wherever another path exists. Before: the fixed watchdog catches grayholes by also accusing honest nodes, and routing around those honest nodes costs delivery; CAD-style accuses fewer but misses grayholes. After: ours judges only what a monitor could observe and expects the normal loss of each link, so it catches the grayholes without accusing honest nodes, and delivery and throughput move back towards the no-attack level.

### Before vs after (live network, all settings pooled)

| method | grayholes caught (%) | honest nodes accused per run | delivery ratio (%) | throughput (pkt/h) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| No attack | 0.0 | 0.0 | 57.0 | 228.6 |

| Fixed watchdog | 100.0 | 7.2 | 47.0 | 190.6 |
| CAD-style | 58.3 | 0.8 | 48.0 | 193.3 |
| Ours | 95.0 | 0.3 | 49.7 | 200.5 |

**fig2_false_accusations.** Honest relays confirmed as suspects by the end of a 6 h run as traffic grows, each method with its own rule (fixed watchdog miss rate > 0.3 (budget 0.6), CAD-style z > 2.0 (budget 2.5), ours alpha 0.0001). 20-node networks, 10 test topologies per point, 95% t-intervals. More traffic means more collisions, which the fixed watchdog mistakes for dropping; ours excludes windows it could not observe and expects the loss each link's distance area normally shows.

**fig3_detection.** Every method judges the same recorded network traffic (6 h, decision every 30 min, a node is a suspect after two flagged rounds in a row), on 10 test topologies. (a) Fair contest: each method's threshold is tuned on 6 separate practice networks (never the test ones) so that at most 5% of honest relays are accused when there is no attacker. (b) Each method with its own rule: the fixed watchdog 'detects' everything only by accusing most honest relays.

**fig4_suspect_list.** (a) What the administrator receives: every judged relay ranked by estimated drop rate = 1 − heard/expected forwards, where expected forwards come from link distances and the normal loss of each link's distance area (Mohit sir's area idea), and the monitors' trust values are averaged weighted by the forwards each expected. The three grayholes rank first and are confirmed; honest relays sit near 0%. (b) Estimated against true drop rate of one grayhole (load 0.005, 10 test topologies, 95% t-intervals).

**fig5_network_performance.** Live network (12 h, 10 test topologies; grayholes = the busiest relays, dropping 30%). Every 30 min each monitor sends one bundled report frame to the sink over the same acoustic channel; the sink runs its detector (each method's own rule), confirms a suspect after two consecutive flagged rounds and routes around it. Report traffic is included. (a) Error bars: 95% t-interval of the difference from 'attack, no defence' on the same topology. (b) Mean over topologies: delivery drops when the attack starts and recovers once traffic avoids the grayholes. (c) The same detectors when suspects are blacklisted (cut out) instead, all settings pooled: every honest node the fixed watchdog accuses is lost together with the nodes behind it, so false accusations collapse delivery. Blacklisting also hurts a correct detector when a grayhole is the only path for many nodes, which is why the response used everywhere else routes around suspects only where another path exists.
